01 · Foreword

A cosy sea, until it is not

You sail the Merry Gull with your first mate Mara through a sunlit, low-poly Caribbean: sail, fish, dig, deliver, chat. The further from home you go, the more the world goes wrong. Nothing is ever explained.

HOIST is drawn the way the games of 1997 were drawn: a small picture blown up big, flat facets, chunky pixels, a little dirt on everything. Every model, texture, sound and wave is made by code at runtime. There is not a single image or model file in the game; the pictures in this book were taken from it as it runs.

"We stopped counting the boats that come back. It was always one more than went out."overheard in a harbour

Five pillars

  • Bright reading first. Every strange thing is first a cosy thing: a baker, a tune, a lamp.
  • Wrongness is repetition and absence. One more than there should be, one fewer, laid for two.
  • Horror by removing and bending. Music loses instruments, colour drains, the wind drops.
  • Chunky, dithered, a little dirty. Low-res 3D and pixel UI on one grid.
  • The world is polite. Patient, kind, and it has already written you down.
02 · The look in numbers

A small picture, blown up big

The whole world is rendered into a picture about 270 lines tall and scaled up with hard nearest-neighbour pixels. One world pixel is about three screen pixels.

270lines tall: the world's real resolution
4×4Bayer dither between every colour step
15-bitcolour, like a cartridge-era console
0lights in the world: light is baked into vertex colours
16tiles in one 256 px atlas, all painted by code
12 fpswater time, stepped on purpose
2,000triangles at most for an island; 3,500 for a hand-made place
4–8sides on every cylinder: low and chunky beats detailed

Rules of the kit

  • Flat-shaded triangle soup built by one Builder: boxes, gables, cylinders, blobs. Things lean a little on purpose.
  • Every model carries a second, darker colour set that the shader slides to as the sea grows strange.
  • Vertices snap to a grid, PS1 style; the snap gets coarser the deeper you go.
  • Grime is part of the look: stained tiles, damp darkening near the waterline, barnacles, rope coils.
  • Glowing texels ignore the light: windows and lanterns shine at night without a single lamp in the scene.
  • Light has classes: steady yellow is friendly, flickering orange is fire, magenta is never friendly.

04 · The Merry Gull

A ship you can read at a glance

She is 6.9 units long and 2.8 wide, with a mast of about 7, and tops out at 11 units a second. The captain never speaks; Mara answers for the ship.

Her parts

  • A cabin, a single mast with a crow's nest, a bowsprit, barrels on deck.
  • Sails are cloth textures from the atlas, reefed by hand; the flag and pennant move with the wind.
  • The stern lantern: an iron frame with a peaked cap, held out over the transom. At night it is the light you sail by, a warm pool on the water.
  • A towed rowing boat and a bell can be fitted; both change how she handles.

Design note: the lantern was chosen from three trial designs: the iron frame, a gallows lamp on a chain, and twin quarter lamps.

05 · Home waters

Harbour Tama

Tama is home: lush grass, sandy paths, picket fences, bougainvillea, and a belfry whose bell rings once at noon. Everything you learn about the sea, you learn here first.

Eight village looks

No two harbours read alike. Each picks one of eight styles (classic, garden, stilt, terraced and others), a custom you can see but nobody explains (whitewash, kites, laundry, bells, statues, silence), and a festival day of its own.

Islands

Sandbars, jungle, rock, treasure isles and harbours, plus rarer volcanoes, atolls and mangroves. Each kind comes in three forms: a dune or a spit, twin peaks or a low canopy, a mesa or a sea arch. Near home, stone is rounded; further out it is cut into blocks.

Budget: one rolled island is at most 2,000 triangles and 4 draw calls. Every place needs a vertical feature of at least 3.5 units, or a light.

06 · The five waters

Every sea has its own manners

Beyond home the sea is shared by four powers, and past them lie the Drowned. Each water has its own water colour, its own ships, its own islands and its own way of being dangerous.

Crown Traders

North. Long clean water, customs piers, ledgers, open sand. Everything is written down.

Free Cays

East. Glassy water over sand, stilt houses, canoes, atolls and mangroves, a night market.

Reef Brotherhood

South-west. Hard rock, schooners, raiders who parley before they fire.

Lantern Guild

West. Lighthouses everywhere, each with its own rhythm; lamps on floats; oil lying in slicks.

The Drowned

The far water. Flat, lead-grey, mud and low sand. Its harbours take no coin.

Home Sound

Tama's own water keeps no region's rules. The safest blue there is.

07 · Sky and weather

Painted clouds, a real moon

The sky

Clouds are painted flat in a few dithered bands, lit from the sun's side. Stars hide behind them and fade into the haze. At sunset, over a clear sea, about one evening in ninety, the last of the sun goes green for one breath.

The moon

She goes round in sixteen days in the real order, rising later each night. How much of her is lit sets how dark the night is. Now and then a full moon turns the colour of an old penny, or the sun goes black at noon.

How far you see

Visibility follows real seas: island peaks at twenty nautical miles on a clear day, a few in drizzle, under a mile in a squall. Just after rain, the air is washed and you see further than ever.

Low water

There are no tides. On the nights round a new or a full moon the sea draws back, and things show that are under water the rest of the month.

08 · The fog and Haven Hesk

It does not stand there. It closes in.

The fog round the Halved Isle is not a shape. Nothing in the world can be seen of it from afar; the scene's own haze thickens over a long way as you sail in, until you are surrounded and the sky is gone. Close to the hull, thin wisps lie on the water in a few soft bands.

Design note: three looks were tried before this one (a ragged wall, drifting veils, a low sea mist); each was still something standing in the sea. The answer was to remove the object entirely.

Inside the bank lies Haven Hesk. Its people went one at a time. Only Hesper, who keeps the light, stayed. Bring her what she asks for and the houses fill, the fog lifts and her beam steadies. Stay away too long, and one day there is only a chair on the lighthouse steps, and a note.

09 · The slide

The same sea, further out

Distance is dread. The sea is cut into six rings, and the same water changes colour as you cross them: first a little off, then wrong, then eerie, then something else.

Home Sound0 to 450
The Shoals450 to 800
Trade Belt800 to 1150
The Slack1150 to 1550
The Dim1550 to 1950
The Lid1950 and beyond
"Do you hear that? No? Good. Me neither."Mara
10 · Interface

Wordless, on the same grid

  • Two typefaces: DotGothic16 for everything, Pirata One for the logo, harbour names and the paper's masthead.
  • A 16 px grid. Nothing below 14 px. No gradients, no blur, no rounded corners, no hairlines.
  • Panels are a dithered navy tile with four hard 4 px edges.
  • The HUD is wordless: gold, the time, the place, and a slip that says what, where, which way and how far.
  • Three bookmarks only: Chart, Orders, Ship's book.
  • Icons are 7×7 character grids, drawn by code and shown three times larger.
11 · People

Who you meet

Mara

First mate. Warm, quick, a little cheeky; one or two short lines; calls you Captain. Cheerful, then steady, then rattled.

The captain

You. Never speaks. People speak at the captain; Mara answers for the ship.

The Lady

A chair in the dark, a bone die, candles, a book. She throws, and writes the numbers down. You throw too.

Old Perrin

The cartographer who never left port. Letters only. Dry, precise, a little smug.

Hesper

Keeps the light at Haven Hesk. Learned to trim a wick from old Sabe of Galra, when he could still see.

The diver

A rusted deep-sea diver standing upright on the water, once. Nothing explains him.

Villagers

Fisher, market woman, old salt, child, docker, harbourmaster: boxy limbs, six-sided bodies, blob heads, and one strong prop each (a hat, a basket, a cane, a crate, a ledger) so they read from the deck. People are about 1.4 units tall: toy-like, never towering over a house.

12 · Colophon

Made of code

HOIST is built with Three.js and Vite. Every island, house, ship, cloud, fish and wave is generated at runtime from a seed; the sounds are synthesised; the textures are painted into one small atlas when the game starts.

Every picture in this book is an unretouched capture from the running game, rendered at its native 270 lines and scaled up.
